title: General DG talk about voice and robotics

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Build a Robot Desk Assistant (4 evenings)

summary: A talk on Deepgram, voice AI and robotics: how a voice agent works, Deepgram's new LLMs and context layer, why voice is the way into robotics, and the Physical AI Lab. Ends with a live Jervis demo. Separate from the four lab evenings.
detail: About 35 minutes of slides plus a Jervis demo, for launch nights and community events. It covers what Deepgram builds, how a voice agent listens, thinks and speaks, turn-taking, how Deepgram compares, the new Think-Live and Think-Fast models, the context layer, function calling, and how the Physical AI Lab robot is built and goes wireless.
outcome: Attendees understand how voice agents work, why voice suits robots, and what they'd build in the Physical AI Lab.
artifact: A free Deepgram key and a reason to sign up for the lab.
prereqs: Nothing. Attendees only need their phone.

slides.title: Robots that talk back
bullets: Revati Naik, San Francisco Chapter Lead, Women in Robotics
Dana Sacco, Senior AI Community Engineer, Deepgram
Talking desktop assistants, an introduction to robot building and animatronics, and an ongoing physical AI lab.

slides.title: I run developer events at Deepgram.
bullets: Tuesdays: labs. Hands-on builds, like the robot lab I'll cover later.
Wednesdays: partner events with partner companies at 505 Howard.

slides.title: Deepgram builds speech-to-text, text-to-speech and voice agents.
bullets: Listen: speech-to-text. Flux for live conversations, Nova-3 for transcription.
Speak: text-to-speech. Flux TTS and Aura-2, built for back-and-forth conversation in many languages.
All together: the Voice Agent API. Listening, thinking and speaking over one connection. This is what runs the robots.

slides.title: Listen, think, speak, on every turn
bullets: Listen: Flux STT turns speech into text and detects when the speaker has finished.
Think: an LLM decides what to say or what action to take.
Speak: Flux TTS turns the reply into speech in the chosen voice.
On the lab robots, the mouth servo moves with the voice.

slides.title: Knowing when someone has finished talking is one of the hardest parts of voice AI.
bullets: Flux detects the end of a thought, not just a pause.
If you interrupt, the agent stops and listens.

slides.title: Three ways to build a voice agent
bullets: One speech-to-speech model: natural conversation, but limited visibility, no own LLM or voice. Keeps tone inside the model.
Separate vendors combined: visibility and your own LLM or voice, but often slower, with integration work. Tone is lost between steps.
Deepgram: built for conversation, visibility and control of each step, your own LLM or voice. Tone carried by the context layer (rolling out).

slides.title: Two models: one for the conversation, one for the task
bullets: Think-Live (conversation): handles backchannels like “mhmm”, tells whether “yeah” means “I agree” or “keep going”, flags when a caller is frustrated. Available in the Voice Agent API, alongside the reasoning LLM you choose.

Think-Fast (tasks): calls tools during the conversation and writes replies meant to be spoken, with numbers and dates as words. Solved 60% of simulated support calls vs 46% for the next-best model its size. Early access on the Deepgram LLM API, with a smaller model, phoneLLM mini.

slides.title: Tone and pace travel with the words
bullets: Cheerful “I'm fine.”, annoyed “I'm fine.”, tired “I'm fine.”: a plain transcript makes all three identical.
The context layer passes tone and pace from speech-to-text to the LLM, and emphasis and pauses from the LLM to text-to-speech.
RCS, the open Real-time Context Standard, is in alpha in Pipecat today. Tone-aware speech-to-text and text-to-speech that follows the markup are coming.

slides.kicker: WHAT THAT MEANS FOR A ROBOT
slides.title: A robot that responds to how you sound, not just what you say
bullets: User sounds upset: slows down and uses a calmer tone.
Room is loud: keeps answers short and confirms what it heard.
User is in a hurry: skips small talk and completes the task.
This is the direction, not all available today. It arrives first in Pipecat, which is open source.

slides.title: Robots don't have keyboards.
bullets: Voice is the natural way to interact with physical AI.

slides.title: Three changes make voice-driven robots practical
bullets: Voice is fast: turn detection and interruptions make conversations feel natural.
LLMs use tools: function calling turns a spoken request into a real action.
Hardware is cheap: a Bluetooth microcontroller costs about $7 and servos cost a few dollars.

slides.title: From a spoken request to a physical action
bullets: User says: “Look to your left.”
LLM calls a function: look_with_eyes(direction: "left")
Robot: eye servos turn left.
The same mechanism voice agents use to book appointments or check the weather.

slides.title: 4 Tuesdays. 1 talking robot each.
bullets: Four Tuesday evenings at 505 Howard.
From the second week, a drop-in study hall on class Tuesdays to catch up, decorate or get help.

slides.title: From a box to a robot that takes actions
bullets: Tue 1, Build + talk: build the box, pick a Deepgram voice, write its personality, and get the mouth moving.
Tue 2, Eyes + personalities: give the servos their own power, add moving eyes, then switch between personalities by voice.
Tue 3, Skills + go wireless: add skills with function calling, then go wireless over Bluetooth or with a Raspberry Pi.
Tue 4, Show and tell: demo your robot to guests.

slides.title: How the robot is put together
bullets: Controller: phone or laptop. Mic, speaker, and the Deepgram voice agent running in a web page.
Microcontroller: Pico W. Receives commands over USB or Bluetooth and drives the servos.
Motion: servos. One for the mouth, two for the eyes, and an optional neck.

slides.title: Getting the robot off the laptop
bullets: Wi-Fi: needs network setup and a relay server. A phone still runs the voice.
Raspberry Pi: works, but costs more per robot.
Bluetooth: built into the Pico W. No setup or server.
54 ms median round trip from phone to robot, with no visible delay in mouth sync (Android with Chrome, robot on a wall charger, no laptop). iPhone with the free Bluefy app is still being tested.

slides.title: Skills you can turn on
bullets: Information skills: weather, Deepgram SF events, timers, notes, next Muni bus, Wikipedia look-up, dice, coins, pick-one.
Body skills: cross eyes, look left / right, or write your own.
Information skills call live data, like Muni arrival times. Body skills move the robot's servos. Developers can add their own.

slides.title: This is the first lab in an ongoing series.
bullets: The plan is to keep running robot labs throughout the year, each with a new robot.

slides.kicker: A POSSIBLE NEXT LAB: ROBOTS THAT SEE
slides.title: With a camera, the voice agent can describe what's in front of it
bullets: Accessibility: help blind and low-vision people read menus and signs, and describe their surroundings.
Finding things: remember where objects were last seen, like keys.
Reading help: read a book page aloud with a child.
Front desk: greet visitors and give directions.
Privacy built in from the start: ask before using the camera, and store nothing that isn't needed.
